difficulties.response: Show the higher-order demands of open-book questions and the time cost of searching.

difficulties.pattern: Copying from notes, slides or sources without attribution under time pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed strings matching lecture slides or readings in submitted answers.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to prepare notes that already separate quotation, paraphrase and own words, and clarify the paper's citation expectations.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a take-home or online exam like coursework: discussing answers with peers or using AI tools that the paper does not permit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Similar answers from students who studied together; questions after the exam about whether a tool was allowed.
difficulties.response: Make each paper's collaboration and AI rules explicit, show learners where they are stated, and discuss why the boundaries are drawn where they are. Where the rules are unclear, learners should ask before the exam, not after.

difficulties.pattern: 'A 24-hour window means 24 hours of writing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers far beyond the expected length; exhaustion; uploads in the final minutes.
difficulties.response: Point to the expected working time where the paper states one, plan a schedule with breaks inside the window, and submit well before the deadline. Do not assume that everyone can use the whole window: caring, work and time-zone constraints differ.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In your next take-home exam, what are you allowed to use and do, and how will you prepare your materials?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the rules accurately (sources, collaboration, AI), describes organised and indexed materials, and plans to apply rather than reproduce.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows some rules but has no preparation plan, or prepares but is unsure of the rules.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know the rules and plans minimal preparation.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes increasingly use open-book, take-home or online formats in subject modules, and some pre-sessional programmes run timed progression tasks online within a fixed window. In-sessional UG and PGT learners meet these formats across disciplines, with PGT take-home exams often resembling short essays. Rules on AI use, permitted resources and remote invigilation vary by paper and change often; similarity and AI-detection scores do not by themselves establish misconduct, and detection tools have been found unreliable (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023). Remote invigilation can create barriers for some disabled learners and for those without a quiet private space, so learners should know how to request alternative arrangements.
reviewNotes: Rules on take-home exams, especially on generative AI, vary widely and are changing rapidly; teach learners to check paper-specific rules rather than presenting general rules.
No bibliography source specifically evaluates open-book exam preparation; guidance here is practitioner-based.

guidance.summary: Oral assessments in higher education vary along several dimensions, including what is assessed, how interactive the event is and how structured it is (Joughin, 1998), so preparation must start from the specific format. Horwitz et al. (1986) identified fear of negative evaluation and communication apprehension as components of foreign language anxiety, which oral exams can intensify. Teach learners to anticipate question types, use a direct-answer structure, ask for clarification and recover from breakdowns, and rehearse with realistic follow-up questions rather than memorised scripts.

activities.title: Mock oral with question types
learnerActions: List likely question types for your oral assessment (clarification, justification, challenge, extension)
Prepare flexible bullet-point answers, not scripts
Take part in a mock oral in which a peer or tutor asks one question of each type
Review a recording and identify one strength and one change
activities.intendedInsight: Preparing for types of question is more robust than preparing scripted answers to predicted questions.
activities.rationale: Oral formats vary in structure and interaction (Joughin, 1998), so rehearsal should include unscripted follow-up.

activities.title: Clarify and hold
learnerActions: Collect your own phrases for asking for repetition, checking meaning and gaining a few seconds of thinking time
Practise them in rapid question rounds with a partner
Discuss when each phrase is appropriate and when it might sound evasive
activities.intendedInsight: Asking for clarification and taking thinking time are legitimate moves, not signs of weakness.
activities.rationale: Having routines for these moves reduces the risk that fear of negative evaluation (Horwitz et al., 1986) leads to silence or guessing.

difficulties.pattern: Memorised scripts break down when the question is unexpected.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent openings followed by long pauses or irrelevant answers to follow-ups.
difficulties.response: Rehearse with unpredictable follow-ups and flexible outlines. Do not ban preparation; change its form.

difficulties.pattern: Freezing or long silence under questioning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence, very short answers, visible distress in mock orals.
difficulties.response: Normalise the experience, rehearse holding and clarification phrases, and use graded practice from low to higher stakes.

difficulties.pattern: Answering a question that has only been partly understood rather than asking for it to be repeated, because asking seems to risk losing marks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that address a misinterpreted question.
difficulties.response: Make explicit that examiners generally expect and accept clarification requests, check whether the format limits them (some test speaking tasks do), and model them. This hesitation is common among novice candidates of all backgrounds.

diagnostic.task: Ask one ambiguous question about the learner's own work and one follow-up challenge.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Asks for clarification of the ambiguous question, answers directly with justification, and handles the challenge by acknowledging and responding.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers the ambiguous question without clarifying, or handles the challenge with long hesitation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot respond to the challenge or answers a different question.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners meet oral assessment in presentations with questions, seminars and speaking assessments; PG-route pre-sessionals often include questioning on the learner's own project. In-sessional UG learners meet orals in language, professional and some science programmes, and PGT learners revisit them where modules use them. The doctoral viva is treated separately (pub.viva). Learners who stammer, are deaf or hard of hearing, or are autistic may need adjustments such as extra time, written questions or a different format; these should be arranged in advance and the assessment should not penalise fluency features unrelated to the construct.
reviewNotes: Oral assessment conventions (permitted notes, whether questions may be repeated, length) differ between formats and institutions; learners should check the rules for each assessment.

guidance.summary: Putwain (2008) conceptualises test anxiety as multidimensional, involving worry and physical and emotional components that arise when evaluative situations are appraised as threatening. Horwitz et al. (1986) identified test anxiety as one component of foreign language anxiety, alongside communication apprehension and fear of negative evaluation, so L2 learners in high-stakes language or content exams may face compounded pressure. Ramirez and Beilock (2011) found that brief expressive writing about test worries before an exam improved anxious students' performance. Present anxiety management as a normal skill, combine it with preparation, and refer severe cases to appropriate services.

activities.title: Worry writing before a mock test
learnerActions: Before a mock test, spend a few minutes writing freely about any worries you have about it
Take the mock test
Afterwards, note whether the writing changed how you felt or performed
Decide whether to use the technique before a real exam
activities.intendedInsight: Putting worries on paper may free attention for the task.
activities.rationale: Ramirez and Beilock (2011) reported benefits of expressive writing for anxious test takers; this classroom version is a proposal to try, not a guaranteed intervention.

activities.title: Realistic rehearsal
learnerActions: Take at least one full practice paper under exam conditions (timing, room, no notes)
Note moments of rising anxiety and what triggered them
Plan a response for each trigger, such as starting with a question you are confident about
activities.intendedInsight: Familiarity with exam conditions reduces uncertainty, and planned responses make anxious moments manageable.
activities.rationale: Putwain (2008) links test anxiety to the appraisal of evaluative situations; rehearsal and planned responses address both uncertainty and the sense of being unprepared.

difficulties.pattern: 'Feeling anxious means I'm not ready or not capable.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Catastrophic statements before exams; avoidance of mock tests.
difficulties.response: Normalise anxiety, separate the feeling from evidence of preparation, and discuss reinterpreting arousal as readiness.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding mock exams to escape the feeling.
difficulties.revealedBy: Absence from practice tests; no timed practice in revision plans.
difficulties.response: Offer graded exposure, starting with short, low-stakes timed tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Going blank on first reading the paper.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports of losing the first minutes; slow starts.
difficulties.response: Teach a first-minutes routine: breathe, read all questions, start with the one you are most confident about. Do not simply advise learners to 'relax', which gives no actionable step.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What do you do when you feel anxious during an exam?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific techniques used before and during exams and knows where to seek support if needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes a general approach ('try to calm down') without specific steps.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no strategy or describes only avoidance.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners face high-stakes progression decisions and often recent proficiency tests. Foundation learners face their first university exams. In-sessional UG learners benefit from short sessions before exam seasons, linked to wellbeing services and to the institution's process for exam adjustments; PGT learners revisit the topic where exams are used. Speaking-specific anxiety is treated in sem.speaking-anxiety.
reviewNotes: Evidence for brief expressive writing comes mainly from Ramirez and Beilock's (2011) studies; it is presented as something to try, and evidence from other contexts should be checked before stronger claims are made.
Severe anxiety is a matter for wellbeing or disability services; this topic is not clinical guidance.

guidance.summary: Sadler (1989) distinguishes formative assessment, which aims to improve learning, from summative assessment, which reports achievement. Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) argue that formative assessment supports self-regulation only if learners understand the goals and criteria. Learners whose previous assessment was dominated by end-of-year examinations may skip unmarked formative tasks or misjudge weightings. Teach assessment literacy with the learner's actual handbook and briefs rather than generic descriptions, because rules vary by institution and module.

activities.title: Handbook audit
learnerActions: Using a real module handbook, list every assessment task, its type, weighting and deadline
Mark each task as formative or summative
Find the rules on late submission, extensions and resits
Compare your findings with a partner's and resolve any differences by checking the source
activities.intendedInsight: The rules and structure of assessment are written down, but they have to be actively found and interpreted.
activities.rationale: Learners can only use formative opportunities and plan effort if they know the assessment design; Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's first principle concerns clarifying what good performance is.

activities.title: Outcome–task–criteria trace
learnerActions: Choose one learning outcome from a module
Find the assessment task that assesses it
Find the criterion or criteria in the rubric that relate to it
Write one sentence explaining what you must show to meet the outcome
activities.intendedInsight: Outcomes, tasks and criteria are designed to align, so reading them together shows what markers are looking for.
activities.rationale: Sadler argues that learners need to understand the standard being aimed at; tracing alignment makes that standard more visible.

difficulties.pattern: 'If it doesn't count, I won't do it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Low completion of formative tasks; surprise at summative feedback that formative work would have anticipated.
difficulties.response: This is a rational response to assessment designs in which only marked work visibly matters, in any system. Design formative tasks so that they feed the summative one, for example by making formative feedback a required input to the final submission, and show learners the link. Avoid threats.

difficulties.pattern: Confusion between terms such as resit, resubmission, deferral and mitigating circumstances.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions that mix the terms; wrong procedures followed.
difficulties.response: Provide a glossary from the institution's own regulations and use the terms in scenarios.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming assessment rules are the same across all modules.
difficulties.revealedBy: Word-limit or referencing rules from one module applied to another.
difficulties.response: Have learners compare two modules' rules and note the differences.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'In one of your modules, which piece of work counts most towards your final mark, and what is the first formative opportunity to get feedback before it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the task, its weighting and a specific formative opportunity, and explains how it will be used.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows the main task and weighting but not the formative opportunities.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know the weighting or the assessment structure.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation programmes this is often the learner's first contact with criterion-referenced coursework, so it is taught explicitly. On pre-sessional courses, use the programme's own assessment as the model; PG-route learners can compare it with assessment in their first degree. In in-sessional UG and PGT contexts, work with real module handbooks; PGT learners need this in the first weeks because the first assessments come quickly. Terms and procedures (resits, extensions, special consideration) differ between institutions and national systems, including in EMI and TNE programmes.

guidance.summary: Grade meanings are local conventions: the same number or letter can signal different quality in different systems. In many UK disciplines percentage marks rarely reach the top of the scale, whereas in some other systems high percentages are routine; letter-grade and grade-point systems, ECTS grades and national numeric scales each have their own thresholds and typical distributions. Sadler (1989) notes that grades compress complex qualitative judgements, so learners need to understand the standards behind a mark, not only its number. Teach the scheme of the learner's target context as typical, and send learners to their own programme regulations, which vary.

activities.title: Grade translation discussion
learnerActions: Describe what a 'good' mark looked like in your previous system
Locate the same level of performance on your institution's scale
Discuss in groups why direct numerical conversion can mislead
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can mean very different things in different systems.
activities.rationale: Making differences between systems explicit prevents misreading marks, which can distort motivation and decisions.

activities.title: Band ladder with exemplars
learnerActions: Read three anonymised exemplars awarded marks in different bands
Rank them before seeing the marks
Compare your ranking with the actual bands and identify the differences in quality
activities.intendedInsight: Grade bands correspond to recognisable differences in quality that can be seen in texts.
activities.rationale: Sadler argues that standards are best conveyed through exemplars alongside verbal descriptions.

difficulties.pattern: A mark that is good on the local scale is read as poor because it would be poor on a scale the learner knows (for example, 60% where 60 was a bare pass).
difficulties.revealedBy: Distress at marks that are good by local standards; requests to resubmit passed work.
difficulties.response: Explain local bands with reference to the regulations and show exemplars at each band.

difficulties.pattern: Attending only to the number and ignoring the feedback.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners can report their mark but not the main comment.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to summarise the main comment before discussing the mark.

difficulties.pattern: Using an online conversion table to turn a mark into a grade from another system and treating the result as exact.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners judging success or querying marks with converted grades ('this would be an A at home').
difficulties.response: Explain that conversion tables are approximations made for particular purposes, such as admissions or transcripts, and that the local criteria define quality. Refer to official conversion guidance only where the institution provides it.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You got 58% on a master's assignment at a university that uses UK-style bands. What does that mean, and where would you check?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Recognises a pass in many such schemes, notes that it falls below the usual merit threshold, and says the programme regulations and feedback should be checked.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises a pass but cannot place it relative to other bands, or interprets it only as 'low'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Interprets it through another system's conventions (for example, as a near fail) without checking.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need this before their first marked work; pre-sessional marks may use a different scale from the degree, which should be made explicit. In-sessional UG learners benefit at their first marks; PGT learners often need it in week one, because master's marking conventions can differ sharply from those of their first degree. In transnational and EMI programmes, learners may meet local and partner-institution scales at once (see acu.emi-tne).
reviewNotes: No bibliography source documents marking distributions across systems; claims about mark ranges are framed as typical and should be checked against institutional regulations.

guidance.summary: Sadler (1989) argued that learners need a concept of quality similar to the assessor's, much of which is tacit and best conveyed through exemplars and guided evaluation. O'Donovan et al. (2004) suggest that explicit criteria on their own do not convey standards, and that exemplars and dialogue are needed. Lea and Street (1998) found that terms such as 'argument' and 'structure' carry discipline-specific and often implicit meanings. Teach criteria through exemplar analysis and discussion rather than by reading the rubric aloud.

activities.title: From criterion to question
learnerActions: Take each criterion in the rubric for your next assignment
Rewrite it as a question you could ask of your own draft (for example, 'Does each paragraph evaluate the sources it cites, or only report them?')
Compare your questions with a partner's and agree a shared list
Check the list with the tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Abstract criteria become usable when turned into concrete questions about a text.
activities.rationale: Sadler argues that learners must be able to apply the standard to their own work; questions make criteria applicable.

activities.title: Exemplar ranking with justification
learnerActions: Rank three short exemplar extracts on one criterion
Justify each ranking with a specific feature of the text
Compare your ranking with the tutor's and discuss any disagreement
activities.intendedInsight: Differences between bands correspond to visible features of texts, which can be learned.
activities.rationale: O'Donovan et al. suggest that combining criteria with exemplars and dialogue conveys standards better than criteria alone; Carless and Boud (2018) also identify exemplar analysis as a feedback-literacy activity.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means criticising the authors.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Texts that list weaknesses of sources with no balanced evaluation.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars in which criticality appears as evaluation, comparison and positioning, and contrast them with fault-finding.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the rubric as a checklist of features to include ('add a counter-argument'), producing formulaic texts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Features present but not doing their job, such as a counter-argument mentioned and then ignored.
difficulties.response: Ask what each feature is for in this text, and use exemplars in which the same feature works well and badly.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming criteria terms mean the same in every discipline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applying, for example, humanities expectations of 'argument' to a lab report.
difficulties.response: Compare how two departments describe the same criterion and discuss with subject staff where possible.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain what one criterion in their next assignment's rubric means and what it would look like in their text.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains the criterion with concrete textual features and distinguishes it from the adjacent band.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Paraphrases the criterion accurately but cannot say what it looks like in a text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the criterion wording or gives a general impression.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation courses introduce rubrics alongside assessment literacy. Pre-sessional courses teach this intensively with their own rubrics: UG-route courses focus on adjacent-band differences in the programme's criteria, while PG-route courses add exemplars of master's-level criticality and source use. In-sessional UG and PGT learners need it applied to disciplinary rubrics, ideally with subject exemplars; PGT learners may find master's-level expectations of criticality very different from their previous experience.

guidance.summary: Carless and Boud (2018) define student feedback literacy in terms of appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect and taking action, and identify enabling activities such as peer feedback and analysing exemplars. Hattie and Timperley (2007) distinguish feedback at the task, process, self-regulation and self (person) levels, and argue that feedback directed at the person is least useful for learning. Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) frame feedback as support for self-regulation. Teach feedback as a process learners take part in, not a product they receive.

activities.title: Feedback type sort
learnerActions: Collect feedback comments from your recent work (or use a set provided)
Sort them into task, process, self-regulation and personal comments
Discuss which types could help with your next, different assignment
Rewrite one vague comment as a question you could ask your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Comments about process and self-regulation carry over to other tasks, while praise of the person gives little direction.
activities.rationale: Hattie and Timperley's levels give learners a way of seeing which feedback is most useful beyond the immediate task.

activities.title: Feelings first, then actions
learnerActions: Read a piece of critical feedback and write down your immediate reaction honestly
Leave it for a day
Reread it and write three things it asks you to do
Discuss with a partner how your view of the feedback changed
activities.intendedInsight: An emotional response to feedback is normal, and creating some distance helps you use it.
activities.rationale: Managing affect is one of Carless and Boud's four features of feedback literacy; the activity makes that process explicit.

difficulties.pattern: 'Feedback is the teacher correcting my mistakes', where previous feedback was mainly correction.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners look only for corrections and disregard comments, questions or peer input.
difficulties.response: Show the range of feedback sources and types, and make clear that most useful university feedback is not correction.

difficulties.pattern: Defensive or deflated reactions to critical comments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dismissing feedback ('the marker didn't understand') or withdrawal after a low mark.
difficulties.response: Normalise the reaction, build in delay before responding, and separate comments about the work from the person. Do not soften feedback into vagueness, which removes the information learners need.

difficulties.pattern: Reading only the mark.
difficulties.revealedBy: VLE data showing feedback unopened; inability to recall comments.
difficulties.response: Release marks after learners have responded to the feedback, where possible, or require a short response to feedback in class.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What was the most useful piece of feedback you've had this term, and what did you do with it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific feedback (not necessarily from a tutor), explains why it was useful, and describes an action and its result.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recalls feedback but has not acted on it, or acted without understanding why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot recall feedback, or refers only to the mark.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit work on what feedback is and how to use it. In-sessional UG and PGT learners need it embedded in module cycles. PGR researchers deal with supervisory and peer-review feedback, where affect and negotiation matter more and the boundary between feedback and disagreement is less clear. For teachers, the topic also implies designing feedback as a dialogue that learners take part in (Carless & Boud, 2018), not only as comments returned with marks.

guidance.summary: Sadler (1989) argued that feedback only improves learning when the learner acts to close the gap between current and desired performance. Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) list providing opportunities to close the gap among their principles, and Winstone et al. (2017) identify learner recipience processes (self-appraisal, assessment literacy, goal setting and self-regulation, engagement and motivation) that affect whether feedback is used. Help learners to group comments, identify recurring themes and transfer process-level advice to different tasks; one-off responses to single comments rarely change practice.

activities.title: Feedback portfolio and theme coding
learnerActions: Gather feedback from your last three pieces of work into one document
Code each comment by theme (for example structure, source use, argument, accuracy)
Identify the two most frequent themes
Write one action for each theme to apply in your next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Recurring comments across assignments show what to prioritise.
activities.rationale: Collating feedback across tasks supports the self-appraisal and goal-setting processes that Winstone et al. associate with using feedback.

activities.title: Feedback response cover note
learnerActions: Before submitting your next draft, write three sentences explaining which previous comments you have addressed and how
Attach the note to the draft
After receiving feedback, check whether the marker noticed the change
activities.intendedInsight: Making your actions on feedback visible helps both you and the marker see whether they worked.
activities.rationale: A cover note creates the opportunity to close the gap that Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick recommend, and opens a feedback dialogue.

difficulties.pattern: 'That comment was about that essay; the next assignment is different.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The same process-level comments recurring across different task types.
difficulties.response: Show how process comments generalise by placing comments from different tasks side by side.

difficulties.pattern: Acting on surface comments (typos, formatting) and ignoring global ones (argument, structure).
difficulties.revealedBy: Revised drafts with corrected errors but unchanged structure.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to prioritise comments by their likely effect on the mark using the criteria. Do not respond by marking only global issues, which leaves learners without information about accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: Vague comments such as 'needs more depth' feel impossible to act on.
difficulties.revealedBy: Action plans that repeat the comment ('add more depth').
difficulties.response: Teach learners to translate vague comments using the criteria and to ask for clarification or an example.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show where in their latest draft they acted on a previous comment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Points to a specific change, explains the comment it responds to and judges whether it worked.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Points to a change but cannot link it clearly to the comment, or made only surface changes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify any change made in response to feedback.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses with draft–feedback cycles provide the main practice, and this is core on both UG- and PG-route courses. Foundation and in-sessional UG learners need to learn to carry feedback across modules. PGT learners often receive feedback after the next assignment is due, so carrying advice forward to a different task is essential. PGR researchers act on supervisory feedback across chapter drafts (see res.supervision).

guidance.summary: Whether written corrective feedback helps was famously contested: Truscott (1996) argued that grammar correction is ineffective and potentially harmful, and Ferris (1999) replied that this conclusion was premature and depended on the quality of correction. Later research reviewed by Bitchener and Ferris (2012) and the meta-analysis by Kang and Han (2015) suggest that WCF can improve accuracy, with effects varying across learner and context factors. Learners' engagement (noticing, understanding and applying corrections) appears central. Teach the course's codes, require a response to them, prioritise recurring categories and connect the work to self-editing.

activities.title: Code, correct and explain
learnerActions: Receive a draft with errors marked by code
Correct each error and write a one-line explanation of the rule or pattern
Check uncertain corrections with a grammar reference or the tutor
Submit the corrected version with your explanations
activities.intendedInsight: Working out why something is wrong is more useful than copying a correction.
activities.rationale: Indirect feedback requires learners to process the error, which links to the role of noticing in acquisition (Schmidt, 1990); whether indirect feedback outperforms direct feedback is not settled (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012).

activities.title: Error log and focused editing pass
learnerActions: Tally coded errors from your last three texts by category
Identify your top two categories
In your next draft, do one editing pass for each of those categories only
Compare the number of errors in those categories with your previous texts
activities.intendedInsight: Your errors are patterned, and targeted checking reduces them more than general rereading.
activities.rationale: Focusing on a limited set of recurring categories reflects arguments for focused feedback and supports the shift from teacher correction to self-monitoring (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: 'I copied the corrections into my final version, so I've fixed it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Corrected drafts followed by the same errors in new texts.
difficulties.response: Require application in new writing and track error categories across texts, not only within one draft.

difficulties.pattern: Being unable to interpret codes because the grammatical terms are unfamiliar.
difficulties.revealedBy: Wrong corrections of coded errors; questions such as 'What is a clause?'
difficulties.response: Teach the metalanguage behind the code with examples from the learner's own writing. Do not abandon codes in favour of direct correction for all errors simply because the terms are new.

difficulties.pattern: Feeling overwhelmed when every error is marked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts covered in marks; learners say they do not know where to start.
difficulties.response: Use focused feedback on priority categories and say which have been marked. Avoid comprehensive marking with no prioritisation.

diagnostic.task: Give three coded errors from the learner's own text and ask them to correct and explain each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Corrects all three and explains the rule or pattern, noting whether each recurs in their writing.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects them but cannot explain why, or explains them but corrects inaccurately.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot interpret the codes or makes incorrect changes.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses use correction codes intensively; on UG-route pre-sessionals, where entry levels are often lower, this is core and should be established early and linked to error logs. In in-sessional UG and PGT contexts, language feedback from subject markers is often sparse or inconsistent, so learners need self-monitoring routines rather than reliance on correction. Automated feedback tools give a further source of correction that learners should weigh in the same way. For learners with dyslexia, spelling-related categories may be better handled with assistive tools than with error logs alone.
reviewNotes: The WCF debate is not fully settled; claims about the relative efficacy of direct versus indirect and focused versus unfocused feedback vary across studies and should not be presented as definitive.
Most WCF studies target a small number of rule-governed structures, so generalising to all error types requires caution.

guidance.summary: Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) emphasise dialogue around feedback, which depends partly on students initiating it. Requests to staff carry a high imposition, and research on student emails to faculty has found that direct, unmitigated requests can be perceived as impolite (Economidou-Kogetsidis, 2011; Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007). Teach learners to make requests specific (what feedback, on what, why) and pragmatically appropriate, and to check what is permitted before submission.

activities.title: From vague to targeted request
learnerActions: Read a vague request ('Can you check my essay?')
Rewrite it to name the specific aspect, what you have already done, and a question
Add appropriate opening, mitigation and closing
Compare versions in groups and discuss what makes a tutor more likely to respond usefully
activities.intendedInsight: Specific, well-framed requests produce more useful feedback and are easier for staff to answer.
activities.rationale: Research on student emails shows that the framing of requests affects how they are perceived; specificity also makes feedback more actionable.

activities.title: Clarification conversation role-play
learnerActions: Choose a comment on your work that you do not fully understand
Prepare two clarifying questions, for example asking for an example of what improvement would look like
Role-play an office-hours conversation with a partner playing the tutor
Swap roles and give feedback on clarity and politeness
activities.intendedInsight: Asking a tutor to clarify feedback is legitimate and can be done respectfully.
activities.rationale: Dialogue about feedback is one of Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's principles; rehearsal reduces the social barrier to starting it.

difficulties.pattern: Not asking for feedback because the rules on what tutors may comment on before submission, and through which channel, are unclear or differ between modules.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unclear comments never followed up; consultation hours unused; requests sent to the wrong person or too late.
difficulties.response: Make the local rules explicit: what tutors may comment on before submission, through which channel, how far ahead, and whether consultation or office hours exist. These differ between institutions and modules, and in some EMI and TNE settings contact runs through other channels. Programmes should state the rules in module materials; learners should check them before asking.

difficulties.pattern: Requests that are too direct (imperatives, demands for quick replies) or so indirect that the request is unclear.
difficulties.revealedBy: Emails such as 'Please check my essay and reply soon' or long apologies without a clear request.
difficulties.response: Where learners' L1 conventions signal politeness through markers such as 'please' attached to direct forms, or through extended deference, show how English academic emails typically mitigate requests with conditionals, modal verbs and acknowledgement of imposition. Present this as a convention for this context, not as more polite in absolute terms.

difficulties.pattern: Asking 'Is this good?' rather than a specific question.
difficulties.revealedBy: General requests that receive general answers.
difficulties.response: Link requests to criteria and ask learners to frame questions around one criterion.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to draft a two-sentence request for feedback on their current assignment plan.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the specific aspect, shows prior work, includes appropriate mitigation, and respects timing.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Is polite but general, or specific but too direct.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Is a general request for checking, or would not ask.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners practise in a low-stakes setting with EAP tutors. In-sessional UG and PGT learners must work with subject staff and varying pre-submission rules. For PGR researchers, seeking and negotiating feedback is central to supervision and links to working with supervisors and responding to reviewers.
reviewNotes: Rules on pre-submission feedback vary widely between institutions and modules.

guidance.summary: Andrade and Valtcheva (2009) describe self-assessment as a formative process in which students reflect on the quality of their work against explicit criteria and revise accordingly, distinct from self-grading. Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found that L2 writers who gave peer feedback improved their own writing more than those who only received it. Sadler (1989) argues that evaluative expertise develops through guided experience of judging work. Structure peer review around criteria, and use calibration (comparing learner and tutor judgements) to build evaluative judgement over time.

activities.title: Calibration rounds
learnerActions: Rate your draft on two criteria before submitting, giving evidence for each rating
Compare your ratings with the tutor's after marking
Explain any gap: what did you notice or miss?
Track your gap over several assignments
activities.intendedInsight: Your judgement of quality can become more accurate with practice and comparison.
activities.rationale: Sadler argues that learners need to develop evaluative expertise; comparing self-ratings with expert ratings provides the information needed to calibrate.

activities.title: Give-to-get peer review
learnerActions: Review a peer's draft using two criterion-based questions
For each issue, say what it is, its effect on the reader and a suggested direction
Note one thing from reviewing their draft that you will apply to your own
Revise your own draft before reading the feedback you received
activities.intendedInsight: Reviewing others' work improves your own writing, not only theirs.
activities.rationale: Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found that giving feedback benefited reviewers' writing; criterion-based prompts help focus comments beyond surface correction.

difficulties.pattern: 'Peers aren't experts, so their feedback is useless.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Peer comments ignored; reluctance to review.
difficulties.response: Emphasise the benefit to the reviewer and structure the review so that comments are useful. This doubt is common among students in any system. Do not make peer review a substitute for tutor feedback.

difficulties.pattern: Peer comments limited to praise and grammar corrections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comments such as 'Good essay' and lists of typos.
difficulties.response: Provide criterion-based question prompts and model higher-level comments.

difficulties.pattern: Self-ratings consistently far above or below tutor ratings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large calibration gaps that persist across assignments.
difficulties.response: Make the gap the focus of discussion: which features did the learner overlook or overvalue? Do not use self-assessment scores towards grades, which encourages inflation.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to give one piece of feedback on a peer's paragraph using a given criterion.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies a specific issue linked to the criterion, explains its effect on the reader and suggests a direction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies an issue but gives no explanation or direction, or comments only on surface features.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives only general praise or general criticism.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses can run regular peer review with scaffolds; on PG-route pre-sessionals it is core, because evaluative judgement of one's own and others' work is expected from the start of master's study. In-sessional UG and PGT learners apply the skill to their own drafts, often without tutor support. PGR researchers use it in writing groups and later in reviewing for journals, where evaluative judgement is a core academic skill.

guidance.summary: Flavell (1979) distinguishes metacognitive knowledge (about persons, tasks and strategies) from metacognitive experiences, and EAP listening pedagogy has shown the person–task–strategy distinction to be a practical teaching frame (Vandergrift & Goh, 2012). Make the three variables explicit, then repeatedly set learners' predictions against evidence, because judgements of learning tend to be driven by fluency and familiarity rather than by how well material can later be retrieved (Bjork et al., 2013). Metacognitive knowledge is built through reflection on real tasks, not delivered in a single lecture.

activities.title: Predict–test–explain
learnerActions: Predict what percentage you will get on a ten-item retrieval quiz on last week's material
Take the quiz without notes
Compare your prediction with your result; the class pools anonymised prediction–result pairs on a scatter plot
Explain your gap under three headings: myself, the task, my strategy
Choose one change to your study approach and repeat the cycle next week
activities.intendedInsight: Feeling familiar with material is not the same as being able to retrieve or use it, and predictions can be made more accurate with evidence.
activities.rationale: Calibration exercises make the gap between judgement and performance visible, which is the information metacognitive knowledge is built from; the tendency to overrate learning after restudy is reviewed by Bjork et al. (2013).

activities.title: Task anatomy comparison
learnerActions: Read two real assessment briefs from your programme that differ in type (for example, a timed exam and a source-based report)
List what each requires: sources, time, genre, criteria, individual or group work
Compare each list with how you usually prepare
Write a three-line 'task knowledge' note for each task stating what preparation it needs
activities.intendedInsight: Different tasks demand different preparation; a single habitual study routine does not fit all of them.
activities.rationale: Flavell's task variable concerns knowledge of how task demands affect what one should do; making it explicit with authentic briefs links metacognition to task analysis.

difficulties.pattern: 'I've read it three times, so I know it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident predictions followed by low recall on self-tests; study logs dominated by rereading and highlighting.
difficulties.response: Use repeated predict–test cycles so learners see the pattern in their own data. Do not simply tell learners that rereading is ineffective: the claim is usually accepted in principle and ignored in practice unless they experience the gap.

difficulties.pattern: Learners describe themselves through fixed labels ('my grammar is bad', 'I'm a visual learner') that close down strategy choice.
difficulties.revealedBy: Self-descriptions without evidence; resistance to trying strategies that do not fit the label.
difficulties.response: Replace labels with specific, evidence-based descriptions (for example, 'in my last two essays my most frequent error was a missing article before singular countable nouns'). Treat a learning-style label as a claim to test against the learner's own results, not as a reason to avoid a strategy, and choose strategies to fit the task.

difficulties.pattern: Learners who have had few occasions to talk about how they learn (for example, on fully teacher-planned or exam-driven courses) have little vocabulary for it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers such as 'I just study' or 'I follow the teacher' when asked how they prepare.
difficulties.response: Provide and model metalanguage (task, strategy, evidence, monitoring) through teacher think-alouds on a real task, and give sentence frames for early reflections. Treat this as unfamiliarity with a way of talking, not a lack of capability.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Which of your study methods last week worked best, and how do you know?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific method and task, cites evidence (a self-test result, feedback, a mark) and notes a limitation or condition.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a method with a justification based on how it felt ('it was easier', 'I understood it').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot name a method, or attributes success only to effort, luck or the teacher.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, introduce the person–task–strategy frame explicitly and link it to the transition from school learning. At later stages the topic is revisited rather than retaught: on pre-sessional courses, attach it briefly to weekly tasks and the progression assessment, and in in-sessional UG and PGT provision, use it before the first assessment cluster or exam season.
reviewNotes: Calibration evidence is mainly from L1 laboratory and classroom studies; its transfer to L2 academic literacy tasks is plausible but less directly tested.

Review response: R4-08 asked for a verified source for the learning-styles statement. The bibliography has none, so difficulties[1] no longer states a research claim and instead treats style labels as claims to test against evidence; if Pashler et al. (2008) is added to the bibliography, the evidence statement can be restored with that citation.

guidance.summary: Zimmerman (2002) presents self-regulation not as a fixed trait but as self-directive processes that learners can acquire, organised into forethought, performance and self-reflection phases, and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) frame feedback as information that serves this cycle. Holec (1981) defines autonomy as the capacity to take charge of one's own learning across objectives, content, methods, monitoring and evaluation, and Benson (2011) stresses that it is developed, situated and a matter of degree. Teach the model briefly at foundation level, then use it repeatedly as a lens on real task cycles while progressively handing learning decisions over to learners; using the model matters more than reciting it. Differences in how readily learners take control reflect their previous opportunities to exercise it, not fixed dispositions.

activities.title: Task cycle post-mortem
learnerActions: Take a returned assignment and list what you did before starting, while working, and after receiving the mark
Map each action onto forethought, performance or self-reflection
Identify the phase where least happened and sort your explanations for the outcome into controllable and uncontrollable causes
Write one if–then plan for that phase in your next task
activities.intendedInsight: Weak outcomes can usually be traced to a specific phase of the cycle, and explaining them through strategy rather than fixed ability points to what to change next.
activities.rationale: Zimmerman's cyclical model locates learning problems in particular sub-processes, and attributing outcomes to strategy use is associated with adaptive rather than defensive reactions in the self-reflection phase.

activities.title: Handover ladder
learnerActions: For a recurring course task (for example, a weekly reading-to-write task), choose the text yourself in week 1
In week 2, also choose the language focus; in week 3, also decide how your work will be evaluated and by whom
Keep a brief record of each decision and its result
At the end, evaluate in two minutes what worked, what you changed and what you will continue to decide for yourself
activities.intendedInsight: Control over learning decisions can be taken step by step, covering goals, materials, methods and evaluation, and each step brings both freedom and responsibility.
activities.rationale: Holec's account of autonomy covers deciding objectives, methods and evaluation, and Benson describes autonomy as developing through supported opportunities to exercise control; staged handover provides those opportunities with support still available.

difficulties.pattern: 'Self-regulation just means being disciplined and studying more hours.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans that increase hours without changing methods; frustration when more time does not improve results.
difficulties.response: Use cases in which more hours did not help and ask learners to find what was missing (monitoring, strategy change, use of feedback). Present regulation as adjusting what you do, not only how long you do it.

difficulties.pattern: Equating autonomy with working alone, and therefore avoiding peers, tutors and support services.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to ask questions or join study groups; reports of struggling alone for long periods.
difficulties.response: Present strategic help-seeking and collaboration as autonomous decisions, and model choosing when to ask for help and whom to ask.

difficulties.pattern: After an early low mark, self-efficacy drops and the learner avoids the next task.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late starts, missed tutorials, statements such as 'there's no point'.
difficulties.response: Help the learner attribute the result to strategy, and set a small, near-term goal they can achieve and see. Avoid generic reassurance that is not tied to evidence.

difficulties.pattern: Open 'self-study' is assigned with no structure, choice points or feedback, and learners do little with it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unused self-access time; learners asking for exact instructions for independent work.
difficulties.response: Requests for structure are a reasonable response to unsupported tasks. Teachers should offer structured choices (for example, three texts to choose from) and build in a report-back before opening tasks fully; removing all structure at once tends to produce inactivity rather than autonomy. Do not attribute the pattern to learners' backgrounds.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Think of your last piece of assessed work. What did you do before you started, while you were working, and after you got it back? And what have you chosen to learn recently that no teacher set?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives concrete actions in all three phases, including monitoring during work and an adjustment made after feedback, and describes a self-chosen goal, method and way of judging success.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives detail about the performance phase but little about planning or reflection, or describes self-chosen activity with no goal or evaluation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes only time spent or effort, and only teacher-set work.

guidance.contextNotes: This is a conceptual topic taught explicitly at foundation level, where the cycle and staged handover of decisions are scaffolded within short, repeated tasks. At later stages it is revisited rather than retaught, through the strategic topics (goal setting, independent study, reflective logs): pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply it to real assessment cycles and to choosing what support to use. For PGR researchers, autonomy is a central expectation of the doctorate, negotiated within supervision and treated mainly in res.supervision and res.writing-productivity.
reviewNotes: Self-regulation and autonomy are difficult to measure directly; the mastery evidence relies on reported and observed learning decisions.

guidance.summary: Dörnyei (2009) proposes that L2 motivation is driven by the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self and the learning experience, and argues that future-self images energise behaviour only under certain conditions, including that they are elaborate, plausible, regularly activated and accompanied by procedural strategies. For EAP this means motivational work is not pep talk; it is helping learners build a realistic image of themselves using English in their discipline and tying it to near-term plans. Treat entry-score pressure (an ought-to motivation) as legitimate while recognising that it may fade once the score is achieved.

activities.title: Future academic self portrait
learnerActions: Interview a current student in your field or read your programme handbook
Write a short description of a typical week on your future programme in which you use English (lectures, seminars, lab work, writing)
Identify the three most demanding language situations in that week
Turn each into a goal for this month with one concrete action
activities.intendedInsight: A specific, plausible future self that is linked to present actions is more useful than a general wish to be fluent.
activities.rationale: Dörnyei argues that future-self images need to be elaborate and plausible and to be accompanied by procedural strategies if they are to shape behaviour.

activities.title: After the score
learnerActions: List your reasons for studying English now and mark each as your own aim or an expectation from others
Discuss which reasons will still apply once you have met your entry requirement
Draft a short plan for continuing language development during your first term, naming in-sessional or independent options
activities.intendedInsight: Motivations imposed by an entry requirement end when it is met, whereas university language demands continue.
activities.rationale: The ideal and ought-to selves differ in how far they are internalised; making the difference visible helps learners plan for life after the test.

difficulties.pattern: 'Once I get the score, I'm finished with English.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Disengagement from non-assessed language work; little interest in in-sessional provision.
difficulties.response: Entry systems present English as a threshold to clear, so this view is a reasonable reading of them; institutions can counter it by presenting in-sessional provision as part of degree study. Show the language demands of degree study through authentic materials (lecture extracts, assignment briefs, student comments). Do not dismiss the score goal: it is real and high-stakes, and dismissing it damages trust.

difficulties.pattern: A vivid but implausible ideal self ('native-like English in six months') leads to discouragement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements of frustration despite measurable progress; self-comparison with L1 English-speaking peers.
difficulties.response: Help learners recalibrate towards plausible images of a competent, intelligible multilingual academic user of English, and question the native-speaker benchmark as a target.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Why are you improving your English, and what will you be doing with it a year from now?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a specific future use of English in their field and links it to present learning choices.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a specific external goal (a score, admission) but no picture of later use, or a vague wish to be fluent.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot articulate a reason beyond obligation, or expresses no link between present study and future use.

guidance.contextNotes: Taught explicitly at foundation level, where entry requirements dominate motivation and the task is to connect them to a longer-term academic self. On pre-sessional courses the topic is revisited, mainly through planning for life after the progression decision. In in-sessional UG and PGT contexts, motivation is often shaped by the learning experience in the discipline, so revisit it through concrete language situations from the learner's modules.
reviewNotes: Evidence for the L2 Motivational Self System is largely correlational and questionnaire-based; links between future-self visualisation activities and achievement in EAP specifically are not well established.

guidance.summary: Goal setting is a core forethought process in Zimmerman's (2002) model: specific, near-term goals provide the standard against which learners monitor and evaluate their performance. Psychological research on implementation intentions (if–then plans that specify when, where and how a goal-directed action will happen) indicates that such plans help people act on their goals (Gollwitzer, 1999). In EAP, anchor goals in the learner's own evidence (feedback, criteria, diagnostic results) and review them at fixed points. Goal-setting worksheets completed once and filed achieve little.

activities.title: Evidence-to-goal conversion
learnerActions: Collect three pieces of evidence: two feedback comments and the criterion on which you scored lowest
Turn each into a goal stating the feature, the context, a success indicator and a date
Swap with a partner, who checks whether progress on each goal could actually be observed
Revise any goal that could not be checked
activities.intendedInsight: Useful goals come from evidence and can be checked; vague goals cannot guide action.
activities.rationale: In Zimmerman's model, goals function as standards for self-monitoring; goals that cannot be observed cannot serve that function.

activities.title: If–then planning
learnerActions: For each goal, predict the obstacle most likely to stop you (for example, a lab report due the same week)
Write an if–then plan: 'If [situation], then I will [specific action]'
At the review point, check whether the situation occurred and whether the plan was triggered
activities.intendedInsight: Planning for obstacles in advance makes it more likely that goals survive busy weeks.
activities.rationale: Gollwitzer (1999) reviews evidence that implementation intentions support goal attainment; here the technique is applied to academic study, so its effect should be monitored, not assumed.

difficulties.pattern: Goals are only distant outcomes (a required test score, a target degree result) with no process goals.
difficulties.revealedBy: Goal sheets listing scores or grades only, as in test-preparation courses; no weekly actions.
difficulties.response: Keep the outcome goal but add near-term process goals that lead towards it. Do not dismiss outcome goals, which are often legitimate requirements.

difficulties.pattern: Setting many goals at once and abandoning them all within two weeks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long goal lists with no recorded progress at review.
difficulties.response: Limit learners to one or two active goals at a time. Do not penalise abandoned goals; treat them as information for the next review.

difficulties.pattern: Goals copied from the teacher's suggestions rather than drawn from the learner's own evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Near-identical goals across a class; goals unrelated to the learner's feedback.
difficulties.response: Require each goal to cite the piece of evidence it comes from.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state one current learning goal and how they will know when it has been met.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a specific goal traceable to evidence, with an observable indicator, a date and a planned action.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a relevant goal but with no indicator or action, or an indicator with no clear link to evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: States a general wish ('improve my writing') or an outcome only ('pass').

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from goals tied to progression requirements and weekly tasks. In-sessional learners revisit goal setting using module feedback. PGR goal setting concerns project milestones and researcher development and is treated in res.supervision and res.writing-productivity rather than here.
reviewNotes: Evidence on implementation intentions (Gollwitzer, 1999) comes mainly from health and social psychology rather than from language learning, so its application to academic study is an extrapolation.

guidance.summary: The planning fallacy, the tendency to underestimate how long tasks will take even when past experience suggests otherwise, is well documented (Kahneman, 2011), and procrastination is common among students and is associated with task aversiveness and impulsiveness (Steel, 2007). L2 learners face an additional consideration: reading and writing in English may take longer than in their L1, and their estimates may not allow for this. Teach time management through learners' own estimate-versus-actual data rather than generic tips; the habit of planning and reviewing matters more than any particular tool.

activities.title: Estimate versus actual log
learnerActions: For one week, record your estimated time for each study task before starting
Record the actual time taken
Calculate your average ratio of actual to estimated time for reading and for writing
Apply this correction to your plan for the following week
activities.intendedInsight: Your own past data is a better guide to how long tasks take than your intuition.
activities.rationale: Kahneman recommends correcting the planning fallacy by consulting evidence from comparable past cases (the 'outside view'); a personal log provides that evidence.

activities.title: Backward plan from the brief
learnerActions: Take a real assessment brief and write the deadline at the end of a timeline
Work backwards, adding dated stages: final check, revision, drafting, planning, reading, task analysis
Add buffer time and mark clashes with other deadlines
Compare plans with a partner and justify your time allocations
activities.intendedInsight: Starting from the deadline shows how early work must begin.
activities.rationale: Breaking a distant deadline into dated stages reduces the delay between intention and action; Steel (2007) links procrastination partly to the distance of rewards and deadlines.

difficulties.pattern: 'I work best under pressure', with work routinely started the night before.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late submissions, all-night sessions, drafts with no time left for revision.
difficulties.response: Use estimate-versus-actual data and the quality of revision as evidence. Introduce small first steps with fixed start times. Do not moralise about laziness, which tends to increase avoidance.

difficulties.pattern: Underestimating reading time in English, for example planning to read 30 dense pages in an hour.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unfinished reading, plans that collapse in the first week.
difficulties.response: Have learners time themselves on actual course texts and plan selective reading. Reading rates on dense academic texts are typically far slower than on familiar material, so plans must be realistic.

difficulties.pattern: Treating timetabled contact hours as the whole workload.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weekly plans containing only classes; surprise at the workload before deadlines.
difficulties.response: Make notional study hours explicit using module credit information and show what fills the non-contact time.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show their plan for the next two weeks.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Includes classes, scheduled independent study blocks, staged work on each assessment with buffers, and evidence of adjusting estimates.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Lists deadlines and classes but has no staged work or study blocks.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no written plan, or a plan of deadlines only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need explicit work on weekly planning and the shift from school timetables. Pre-sessional learners manage intense, short courses with stacked deadlines. In-sessional UG and PGT learners must juggle concurrent modules (PGT especially, in a compressed year). PGR time management across long projects is treated in res.writing-productivity, so this topic is not listed for PGR.
reviewNotes: The additional time cost of reading and writing in an L2 is widely reported by practitioners; no specific source from the bibliography is attached to that claim.

guidance.summary: Wingate (2006) argues that learning to learn should be developed within subject learning rather than taught as detached 'study skills', which suggests teaching independent study through real module materials. Benson (2011) shows that autonomy develops through practice in making learning decisions. Make the hidden arithmetic of notional learning hours explicit, then model what productive independent study looks like for particular sessions and assessments. Note that credit conventions differ across systems and institutions, so learners should check their own handbook.

activities.title: Hours arithmetic and audit
learnerActions: Using your module handbook, calculate the expected total study hours and subtract contact hours
Divide the remainder by the number of teaching weeks
Compare the result with the independent study you actually did last week
List what the extra hours should contain for this module
activities.intendedInsight: Most of the expected learning time happens outside class, and it needs content as well as time.
activities.rationale: Making tacit expectations explicit is a precondition for learners being able to meet them; Wingate argues for developing such understanding within the subject context.

activities.title: Before-and-after session plan
learnerActions: Choose one lecture or seminar for next week
Plan preparation: pre-reading, key vocabulary, two questions to bring
Plan consolidation: a summary from memory, self-test questions, follow-up reading
At the end of the week, record what you did and whether the session was easier to follow
activities.intendedInsight: Independent study is most useful when tied to specific sessions and tasks.
activities.rationale: Linking independent work to particular sessions gives learners decisions to make within a structure, which Benson identifies as the way autonomy develops.

difficulties.pattern: 'If there's no homework, there's nothing to do.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Little independent activity between sessions; unpreparedness in seminars; module materials that state study hours but not what should fill them.
difficulties.response: Where courses do not say what independent study should contain, learners reasonably read the absence of set tasks as nothing to do. Make preparation and consolidation tasks visible in module materials and model them, then gradually withdraw explicit instructions.

difficulties.pattern: Independent study consists mainly of rereading lecture slides.
difficulties.revealedBy: Study logs dominated by passive review; weak recall on self-tests.
difficulties.response: Introduce retrieval-based consolidation and show its results in learners' own self-tests.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What did you do last week outside class for one of your modules, and how did it connect to what happened in class?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific preparation and consolidation linked to particular sessions or assessments, with a rough sense of time.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes relevant activity with no clear link to sessions, or a link with no specific activity.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes no independent activity, or only completing set homework.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes often provide the first experience of large blocks of unstructured time, so explicit modelling is essential and the topic is core. Pre-sessional courses can simulate the expectation with scheduled self-access time. PGT learners should apply the approach to their actual modules, where intensity makes planning urgent; in-sessional UG learners revisit it at points of need. Credit conventions differ between systems and institutions, so learners should check their own handbook.
reviewNotes: Credit conventions are given as examples; credit systems differ (for example UK credits, ECTS and US credit hours), and learners should use their own programme's figures.

guidance.summary: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated practice testing and distributed practice as high-utility techniques across learners, materials and tasks, and rated highlighting, rereading and summarisation as typically practised as low-utility. Roediger and Karpicke (2006) found that retrieval practice outperformed restudy on delayed tests even though restudy looked better on an immediate test, and Cepeda et al.'s (2006) synthesis found that spaced practice outperforms massed practice, with longer retention intervals tending to call for longer gaps. These findings support retrieval and spacing themselves, not any particular schedule shape. Most of this evidence concerns content learning by L1 learners; in EAP, apply it explicitly to vocabulary and formulaic language as well as to subject material.

activities.title: Restudy versus retrieve mini-experiment
learnerActions: Take two matched sets of ten academic collocations from your reading
Study set A by rereading it three times; study set B by reading it once and then testing yourself twice from memory
Predict which set you will remember better
Test both sets one week later and compare your results with your prediction
activities.intendedInsight: Retrieving information is a stronger learning event than looking at it again, even though it feels harder.
activities.rationale: The activity reproduces the logic of Roediger and Karpicke's (2006) restudy and testing comparison at classroom scale. Treat class results as an illustration, not as proof.

activities.title: Notes to questions
learnerActions: Write retrieval questions in the margin of your lecture or reading notes
Cover the notes and answer the questions one day later, then one week later, then before the assessment
Mark which answers you got wrong and spend extra time on those items
activities.intendedInsight: Notes become a self-testing tool rather than something to reread.
activities.rationale: This combines practice testing and distributed practice, the two techniques Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated most highly; Cepeda et al. (2006) show that spacing reviews out beats massing them, and the growing gaps here are one reasonable schedule rather than a requirement.

difficulties.pattern: 'Testing myself is for checking at the end, not for learning.' Learners avoid self-testing because errors feel discouraging.
difficulties.revealedBy: Self-testing used only once, just before the exam; reluctance to attempt recall before rereading.
difficulties.response: Present retrieval errors as productive and keep early self-tests low-stakes and ungraded. Show learners their own delayed-test results.

difficulties.pattern: Highlighting and rewriting notes neatly are treated as studying.
difficulties.revealedBy: Colour-coded, carefully copied notes alongside weak recall.
difficulties.response: Do not ban these habits; they are common among students everywhere. Reposition them as preparation for retrieval (for example, highlight only what you will turn into a question).

difficulties.pattern: Abandoning spacing because cramming produces better results on a next-day quiz.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report that cramming 'works' on the basis of immediate tests.
difficulties.response: Test again after a delay so learners see the difference in retention. Do not rely on assertion alone; the immediate benefit of cramming is real, which is why the long-term cost is easy to miss.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe exactly what they did the last time they prepared for a test or quiz.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes self-testing spread over several sessions, with time reallocated to items they got wrong.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses some self-testing, but in a single session or only at the end.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes only rereading, highlighting or copying notes, usually in one session.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit most from explicit work because they will face content exams, so the topic is core there. On pre-sessional courses, apply the techniques mainly to vocabulary and phraseology. In in-sessional UG provision, link them to module content and exam preparation, ideally with subject staff; PGT learners revisit them where modules use exams.
reviewNotes: Dunlosky et al.'s utility ratings rest mainly on studies with L1 learners and content material; their application to L2 vocabulary and academic phraseology is plausible and consistent with vocabulary research but should be presented as an extrapolation.
Whether expanding review intervals outperform equally spaced ones is not settled; the cited studies support spacing and retrieval themselves, so the guidance does not prescribe a schedule shape.

guidance.summary: Oxford's (1990) taxonomy distinguishes direct strategies (memory, cognitive, compensation) from indirect ones (metacognitive, affective, social) and argues that strategies can be taught. Plonsky's (2011) meta-analysis found an overall positive effect of strategy instruction, varying by context and strategy type. Effectiveness depends on how well strategies are combined and fitted to tasks; using more strategies more often is not in itself a sign of a good learner. In EAP, teach strategies explicitly with real academic targets, then model, practise and have learners evaluate them.

activities.title: Strategy cluster for a disciplinary target
learnerActions: Choose a reading from your field and notice ten phrases you could use in your own writing
Record each with its form, meaning, an example and the context in which it appeared
Plan when you will test yourself on them
Use at least three in your next piece of writing and check them with a corpus or dictionary
After two weeks, evaluate which steps helped and which you will keep
activities.intendedInsight: Several strategies working together on one concrete target are more effective than isolated tips.
activities.rationale: Oxford's categories describe complementary strategy types; combining cognitive, memory and metacognitive strategies on one target reflects the emphasis on orchestration rather than frequency of use.

activities.title: Strategy exchange
learnerActions: Try one new strategy for a week
Bring evidence of its effect (a self-test result, a feedback comment, a recording)
Present the strategy and the evidence to a small group in two minutes
Choose one strategy from a peer to try next week
activities.intendedInsight: Strategies should be judged by evidence of their effect, and peers are a source of tested options.
activities.rationale: Plonsky (2011) found that strategy instruction can be effective, and asking learners to evaluate strategies themselves builds the metacognitive judgement needed to continue without a teacher.

difficulties.pattern: 'The more strategies I use, the better learner I am.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Long strategy lists with nothing evaluated; questionnaire answers claiming frequent use of everything.
difficulties.response: Focus on fit and evaluation: ask which strategy served which target and what the evidence was.

difficulties.pattern: Using the L1 or translation is seen either as cheating, where previous classes banned L1 use, or as the only strategy available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hidden use of translation tools, or exclusive reliance on them for all reading and writing.
difficulties.response: Present the plurilingual repertoire as a resource and teach when L1 use helps (securing a concept, planning) and when it may limit development (composing everything through translation).

difficulties.pattern: Strategies practised in class are not used in independent study.
difficulties.revealedBy: Good use during lessons; no trace in study logs or later work.
difficulties.response: Build planned independent application and a report-back into the course. Do not assume that demonstrating a strategy once will lead to transfer.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What do you do when you meet a useful academic phrase in your reading?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes noticing, recording form and use, planned retrieval and trying it in writing, with some check of accuracy.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Records it but has no plan to review or use it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does nothing specific, or only translates it in the margin.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses can teach strategies explicitly with weekly practice, with an eye to continued development after the course. In-sessional UG learners need strategies they can apply to their own disciplinary texts with very little class time, so focus on a small set of high-yield strategies; PGT learners revisit them as needed.
reviewNotes: Strategy taxonomies, including Oxford's, have been criticised for overlapping categories and for relying on questionnaire measures; treat the categories as a teaching heuristic.

guidance.summary: Moon (2004) treats learning journals as tools for deepening learning and notes that reflection ranges from descriptive to deeper levels and needs to be taught rather than assumed. In terms of self-regulation (Zimmerman, 2002), a log makes self-monitoring and self-evaluation visible. Keep entries short, frequent and structured by prompts linked to goals. Assessing logs on length or emotional disclosure tends to produce performative writing rather than learning.

activities.title: Three-line weekly log
learnerActions: Each week write three lines: my goal; what I did and the evidence of its effect; my next step
Every four weeks, reread the entries and highlight any patterns
Revise your goals on the basis of those patterns
