activities.intendedInsight: A short, structured log is easier to keep up and produces evidence you can act on.
activities.rationale: The structure mirrors the self-monitoring and self-evaluation processes in Zimmerman's model, so each entry feeds the next planning decision.

activities.title: From description to analysis
learnerActions: Compare two sample entries about the same week, one descriptive and one analytical
Identify what the analytical entry does that the descriptive one does not (explains causes, cites evidence, decides next steps)
Rewrite one of your own recent entries to make it analytical
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection is useful when it explains and leads to decisions, not when it only reports what happened.
activities.rationale: Moon describes levels of reflective depth and argues that learners need to be shown what deeper reflection looks like.

difficulties.pattern: Writing what the teacher seems to want to read rather than honest evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniformly positive entries; formulaic phrases about 'learning a lot'.
difficulties.response: Graded or closely read logs invite performance for the reader. Keep logs low-stakes, make clear who reads them and why, and value specific evidence over positive tone. Do not grade on depth of disclosure.

difficulties.pattern: Entries list activities without analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Entries such as 'Monday: read chapter 3. Tuesday: wrote paragraph.'
difficulties.response: Add question prompts (Why? What evidence? What next?) and model an analytical entry. Do not simply tell learners to 'be more reflective', which gives no direction.

difficulties.pattern: The log is abandoned when workload rises.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gaps in entries that coincide with deadlines.
difficulties.response: Keep the format minimal, and schedule a brief in-class log slot during busy periods.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud their most recent log entry and say what decision it led to.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The entry links an action to evidence, and the learner names a concrete decision that followed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The entry contains some evaluation, but no decision followed from it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The entry is purely descriptive, or no recent entry exists.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses (UG and PG routes) often require logs or a reflective portfolio as part of progression, so the topic is core there; keep entries short and tied to goals. Foundation courses introduce logs with more scaffolding. In in-sessional UG and PGT contexts, a brief log can be revisited to support work on feedback across modules. Accept audio, video or bullet-point entries where written logs create barriers, for example for some learners with dyslexia. PGR research diaries serve broader purposes (reflexivity, research records) and are not covered here.
reviewNotes: Evidence that learning logs improve language outcomes is mixed and context-dependent; their value probably depends on whether entries feed actual decisions and dialogue with a tutor.

guidance.summary: Support provision has often been framed as remedial, and Wingate (2015) argues for inclusive academic literacy development for all students instead of deficit-based support for some. Sloan and Porter (2010) show that perceptions of in-sessional EAP can change when provision is contextualised and embedded in disciplinary teaching. Present support services as used by successful students, and teach learners how to prepare for an appointment so that the time is productive.

activities.title: Scenario-based service search
learnerActions: In pairs, receive six realistic scenarios (for example, a statistics question, a reference-list problem, a mark you do not understand, ongoing anxiety)
Use your institution's web pages to find the right service and how to book it
Note what each service will and will not do
activities.intendedInsight: Support is specialised, and knowing which service does what saves time and frustration.
activities.rationale: Making provision visible and normal counters the remedial framing that Wingate (2015) identifies as a barrier.

activities.title: Appointment preparation
learnerActions: Prepare a one-page appointment sheet: the task, your specific question, what you have tried, and relevant materials such as the draft, brief or feedback
Role-play the first two minutes of the appointment with a partner
After a real appointment, record two things you learned
activities.intendedInsight: A specific, prepared request gets far more useful help than 'Can you check my essay?'
activities.rationale: Sloan and Porter (2010) show that the perceived value of in-sessional support depends partly on how well it connects to students' actual disciplinary tasks; preparation makes that connection explicit.

difficulties.pattern: 'Using support means I'm failing or weak.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who are struggling but do not book appointments; support sought only after a fail.
difficulties.response: Normalise use by inviting service staff into class and sharing anonymised accounts of strong students who used support.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting a writing or language centre to proofread or correct the whole text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts handed over with a request to 'fix the English'.
difficulties.response: Explain what advisory services do and why, linking to institutional rules on proofreading and authorship.

difficulties.pattern: Unfamiliarity with services that were absent or organised differently in the learner's previous institution.
difficulties.revealedBy: Surprise that such services exist; uncertainty about whom to ask.
difficulties.response: Provide an explicit map of services early and revisit it at points of need such as the first assignment and exam season.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'If you didn't understand a comment on your essay and your tutor was unavailable, where else could you go, and what would you take?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names an appropriate service, how to access it, and specific materials to bring.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a service but has no idea how to prepare, or is unsure what it offers.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot name a service other than the tutor, or would not seek help.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need an explicit map of services before they reach the degree, including disability services and how to request adjustments and assistive technology (see dig.assistive-technology). In-sessional UG and PGT learners revisit it at points of need. PGR researchers' support (doctoral college, researcher development, thesis-writing provision) is treated with supervision and research topics, so this topic is not listed for PGR.

guidance.summary: Zhou et al. (2008) review stress-and-coping, culture-learning and social-identification models of international students' adjustment, which frame difficulties as responses to change rather than personal failings and point to both coping resources and skills that can be learned. EAP teachers are not counsellors: their role is to normalise pressure, help learners plan around predictable workload peaks and refer appropriately. Avoid generic wellness lectures; connect the topic to learners' actual calendar.

activities.title: Term pressure map
learnerActions: Mark every deadline and exam for the next term on a single calendar
Shade the weeks where pressure will peak
For each peak, write two protective actions you will take beforehand (start earlier, reduce other commitments, arrange support)
Revisit the map at mid-term
activities.intendedInsight: Many pressure points are predictable and can be planned for.
activities.rationale: Treating stress as a predictable response to demands, as stress-and-coping models do, shifts attention to planning and coping resources.

activities.title: Who to contact, and when
learnerActions: Sort scenarios by level of concern: everyday stress, persistent difficulty, urgent risk
Match each to an appropriate response or service, including urgent routes
Check your institution's web pages for the actual contact routes
activities.intendedInsight: Different levels of concern call for different responses, and knowing the route in advance makes it easier to act.
activities.rationale: Knowing what support exists is a coping resource in its own right; this activity builds that knowledge before it is needed.

difficulties.pattern: 'Sleep is wasted time before exams.'
difficulties.revealedBy: All-night study before assessments; tiredness in exams.
difficulties.response: Discuss the cost to performance of exhaustion and plan revision so that late nights are not needed. Do not lecture; connect to the learner's own experience of tired performance.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to disclose difficulties or seek help because of stigma or fear of consequences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Disengagement without explanation; sudden drops in attendance or quality.
difficulties.response: Normalise help-seeking, clarify confidentiality where accurate, and make referral routes visible.

difficulties.pattern: Isolation in the first term as previous support networks are no longer close at hand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who rarely speak to peers outside class; reports of loneliness.
difficulties.response: Build structured peer contact into the course, such as study groups, and point to social and community opportunities.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'When is your busiest point this term, and what will you do differently that week?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the peak and names specific protective actions taken in advance.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the peak, but the plan is only to work more.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify the peak or has no plan.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners are often in their first period away from home and on intensive timetables. In-sessional UG learners revisit the topic around first-year assessment clusters, and PGT learners in a compressed year. It is kept for PGR as a revisit only because the PGR situation differs materially (long, unstructured timelines and isolation), with the main treatment in res.writing-productivity and researcher development provision.
reviewNotes: This topic should be taught in coordination with institutional wellbeing services; teachers should not offer clinical advice.
No bibliography source specifically addresses sleep and academic performance; claims about sleep are kept general.

guidance.summary: Mohan (1986) argued that language and content should be integrated because language is the medium of learning in every subject. The systematic review by Macaro et al. (2018) indicates that the language demands of English-medium subject study are substantial and that gains in content and language cannot be taken for granted. Dafouz and Smit (2016) emphasise that English-medium education varies by context, agents and practices. In EAP, help learners anticipate the double load and develop routines for separating, and then connecting, language and concept problems.

activities.title: Language or concept?
learnerActions: Read a passage from a textbook in your subject
Mark each difficulty L (language: word, grammar) or C (concept: unfamiliar idea)
Choose a different repair for each type: dictionary or glossary for L; textbook glossary, L1 source or worked example for C
Explain the passage to a partner and check whether both kinds of difficulty were resolved
activities.intendedInsight: Not every comprehension problem is a language problem, and the repair should match the cause.
activities.rationale: Mohan's integration of language and content implies that learners need to handle both dimensions; separating them first helps learners choose effective repair strategies.

activities.title: Two-level explanation
learnerActions: Choose a key concept from your subject
Explain it in two or three sentences using the technical terms
Explain it again for a non-specialist friend
Compare the two versions: which words changed, and what had to be added?
activities.intendedInsight: Moving between technical and everyday expression shows, and strengthens, understanding of both the concept and the language.
activities.rationale: Maton's (2013) notion of semantic waves describes knowledge-building as movement between abstract, condensed meanings and concrete, simpler ones; this activity asks learners to make that movement deliberately.

difficulties.pattern: Translating every term and still not grasping the concept, especially with sub-technical words (for example, 'significant' or 'power') whose disciplinary meaning differs from the everyday one.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct translations alongside wrong explanations; confusion when the everyday meaning is applied.
difficulties.response: Highlight sub-technical polysemy and require learners to explain concepts, not just translate terms.

difficulties.pattern: 'Content is the subject teacher's job; English is the language teacher's job.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners keep subject and language learning separate and do not apply language strategies to subject texts.
difficulties.response: Use authentic subject texts in EAP lessons and, where possible, co-plan with subject staff.

difficulties.pattern: Overload in early weeks when both content and language are new.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports of understanding 'nothing'; withdrawal in subject classes.
difficulties.response: Pre-teach key terms, encourage strategic L1 use for securing concepts, and build background knowledge before dense input.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a concept from this week's subject teaching and to say what made it difficult.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains the concept accurately using the discipline's terms and distinguishes language from conceptual difficulties.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses the terms correctly but explains the concept vaguely, or explains it well only in the L1.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot explain the concept or attributes all difficulty to 'the English'.

guidance.contextNotes: This topic is core in foundation programmes and central in transnational or English-medium (EMI) contexts where subject content and English are taught together (see acu.emi-tne). On content-based pre-sessional courses it shapes text choice. In-sessional UG and PGT learners meet it when entering a new discipline, and PGT students changing field face a particularly steep double load. For teachers it also implies integrating language work with subject content and, where possible, co-planning with subject staff.

guidance.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) frame assessment as a chain from performance to interpretation to decision, which shows learners that a score matters because of the decision it supports. The CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001) distinguishes types of assessment, including achievement and proficiency assessment, and Murray (2016) discusses post-entry language assessment as a separate purpose from entry testing. Teach purposes through the assessments learners actually face, and address common misconceptions, such as treating a diagnostic task as a test to be gamed.

activities.title: Purpose–decision map
learnerActions: List every language assessment you have taken or will take this year
For each, note its purpose, who uses the result and what decision it affects
Compare maps in groups and identify any assessment whose purpose was unclear
activities.intendedInsight: Each assessment exists to support a particular decision, which affects how you should approach it.
activities.rationale: Bachman and Palmer's assessment use argument links scores to decisions; mapping makes that link concrete for learners.

activities.title: Same score, different decisions
learnerActions: Consider a borderline score and discuss what decisions different users (a university, a placement coordinator, a teacher) might make with it
Discuss why a small score difference may not reflect a real difference in ability
Agree what other evidence could inform each decision
activities.intendedInsight: Scores are evidence with limits, and decisions should take those limits into account.
activities.rationale: Measurement error and the uses made of scores are central concerns in Bachman and Palmer's framework.

difficulties.pattern: 'My score is my level, permanently.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners describe themselves by a score; discouragement or complacency based on a single result.
difficulties.response: Discuss scores as a snapshot with error, and point to development since the test.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a post-entry diagnostic task as high-stakes and preparing to 'pass' it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memorised essays in diagnostic writing; anxiety about results that only guide support.
difficulties.response: Explain the purpose and use of diagnostic results and stress that accurate results lead to more useful support.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting the course achievement mark to equal a proficiency score.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions such as 'What IELTS score is this mark?'
difficulties.response: Explain the difference between what was taught and assessed on a course and general proficiency, and refer to how the institution expresses equivalence where it does.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is the difference between the test you took to apply and the assessments on this course?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes the purposes (general proficiency for admission versus achievement and progression on a course) and the decisions each supports.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes differences in format but not in purpose.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no difference, or describes both simply as 'English tests'.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners face several assessments with different purposes in a short period. In-sessional UG and PGT learners may meet post-entry diagnostic assessment and need to revisit its supportive purpose.

guidance.summary: The CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001, 2020) is a descriptive framework of communicative ability, not a test; the Companion Volume refines and extends the illustrative scales, including plus levels and mediation. North (2014) explains that relating an examination to the CEFR requires specific procedures and expert judgement, so test-to-CEFR alignments are claims made by test owners, not exact conversions. As a UK example, at the time of writing the Student route requires English at CEFR B2 for degree-level study (B1 below degree level), shown through a Home Office-approved secure English language test or, for degree-level study at higher education providers with a track record of compliance, the provider's own assessment, with some nationality and qualification exemptions (UK Visas and Immigration, 2025). Both the requirements and the approved-test arrangements change, so they must be checked at source and visa questions referred to qualified advisers. Arkoudis et al. (2012) argue that meeting entry standards is the start of language development, not its end.

activities.title: Read the requirement
learnerActions: Find the English language requirement for your intended programme
Identify the overall score and any minimum per skill
Check three sample score profiles against it
Note where the institution says its requirement comes from and when it was last updated
activities.intendedInsight: Requirements have several parts, and missing one component minimum can matter as much as the overall score.
activities.rationale: Accurate reading of requirements prevents costly misunderstandings; component minimums reflect the CEFR's recognition that profiles differ across skills.

activities.title: Where is the official rule?
learnerActions: Find the official government guidance on the English requirement for your visa route
Compare it with what an agent website or forum says
Note differences and the date of each source
activities.intendedInsight: Official current sources are the only reliable basis for decisions about requirements.
activities.rationale: Visa requirements change; learning to check the official source is more durable than learning a specific rule.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a test score as an exact CEFR level ('6.5 is C1') or assuming scores convert directly between tests.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners quoting conversion tables as exact; surprise when institutions accept different scores from different tests.
difficulties.response: Explain that alignments are approximate claims by test owners and that institutions set their own requirements. Do not supply a single conversion table as authoritative.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I meet the entry requirement, my English is good enough for my degree.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to engage with in-sessional support after admission.
difficulties.response: Show the language demands of the degree that entry tests do not measure directly, such as extended source-based writing.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on outdated or unofficial information about requirements.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners citing rules that have changed, or advice from agents and social media.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to check dates and official sources, and model doing so.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What English level do you need for your programme, and how do you know?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the requirement including component minimums, names the official source and acknowledges that rules can change.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States the overall requirement but not the component minimums, or cites an unofficial source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Is unsure of the requirement or confuses institutional and visa rules.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners are often under direct pressure from entry and visa requirements, so accuracy and up-to-date sources are essential; reading individual score reports against requirements is treated in tst.score-reports. Teachers should avoid giving visa advice and refer learners to official guidance and institutional advisers.
reviewNotes: Visa rules and accepted tests change; the UKVI reference is dated 2025 and content must be reviewed at each release.
No test-to-CEFR concordance is stated, by design.

guidance.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) describe how task characteristics shape what an assessment measures, which is why preparation should target the constructs behind task types rather than surface tricks. Washback, the influence of tests on teaching and learning, is more complex than often assumed and has to be demonstrated rather than presumed (Alderson & Wall, 1993), and Green's (2007) study of IELTS preparation documents how test-focused preparation can narrow attention to test task types. Teach formats at the level of task types and constructs, using official current sample materials and public criteria, and do not reproduce test content. Formats and timings change, so learners should check the test owner's current information.

activities.title: Construct mapping
learnerActions: Using official sample tasks, list each task type in your test
For each, write what skill or ability you think it is trying to measure
Discuss which university activities draw on the same ability
activities.intendedInsight: Each task measures something, and preparing for that ability is more useful than preparing for the task's surface.
activities.rationale: Focusing on constructs rather than task tricks reflects Bachman and Palmer's account of task characteristics and may reduce the narrowing effects of washback that Green (2007) describes.

activities.title: Criterion paraphrase
learnerActions: Find the public names of the scoring criteria for the writing or speaking tasks
Explain each criterion in your own words
Identify which criterion your recent practice responses meet least well
activities.intendedInsight: Scores for productive tasks rest on several criteria, so preparation should address all of them.
activities.rationale: Knowing the criteria directs preparation towards what is assessed; criterion names are public, but descriptor text should not be reproduced in class materials.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on unofficial templates and 'tricks' learned from preparation materials.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memorised phrases and structures; claims about secret rules for scoring.
difficulties.response: Compare the tricks with official criteria and samples, and show their limits. Do not ridicule the learner's preparation; it often reflects the market they had access to.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming all academic tests have the same format.
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparing for one test with another's materials.
difficulties.response: Compare task types across two tests at the level of constructs.

difficulties.pattern: Using outdated information about formats.
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparing for tasks or timings that no longer apply.
difficulties.response: Direct learners to the test owner's current official information.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe the speaking section of the test they will take and what it scores.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes task types accurately, names the scoring criteria and explains them.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes tasks accurately but not the criteria, or vice versa.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives an inaccurate or trick-based description.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners may be preparing for, or have recently taken, a test. Emphasise constructs and official sources, and connect test preparation to broader academic literacy development rather than replacing it. Task types, timings, delivery modes and score scales change (several major tests have been redesigned in recent years), so check the test owner's current task list before teaching any task-specific strategy, including for integrated tasks (see syn.integrated-tasks).
reviewNotes: Test formats, timings and delivery modes change; this topic deliberately avoids specific timings, item counts and named task lists.
IELTS criterion links were removed so that the topic does not imply a preferred test (R6-11).

guidance.summary: Moore and Morton (2005) compared IELTS Task 2 prompts with university writing assignments and found that university writing typically draws on sources and spans varied genres, whereas the test task relies on prior knowledge and opinion and more closely resembles certain public, non-academic genres. Horowitz (1986) found that university tasks mostly require selecting and reorganising material from sources. Green (2007) documents how test-focused preparation can narrow attention to test task types. Make the differences explicit so that learners can set aside test habits that do not serve them, without dismissing the test skills that transfer.

activities.title: Two-task comparison grid
learnerActions: Place a test writing prompt and a university assignment brief side by side
Compare them on length, sources, audience, genre, time and criteria
Identify which test skills transfer (for example, paragraph organisation) and which do not (for example, unsupported opinion)
activities.intendedInsight: Some test skills transfer, but university writing makes different demands, above all for using sources.
activities.rationale: The grid operationalises the dimensions of difference identified by Moore and Morton (2005).

activities.title: Template audit
learnerActions: Highlight memorised phrases and structures from test preparation in one of your recent texts
Decide for each whether it suits an academic text in your field
Replace those that do not with alternatives found in disciplinary texts
activities.intendedInsight: Phrases that score well in a test can sound formulaic or out of place in university writing.
activities.rationale: Green (2007) shows how test preparation shapes learners' language and attention; auditing makes these effects visible and revisable.

difficulties.pattern: Using memorised test templates (for example, a fixed introduction formula) in university assignments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Identical openings across assignments; formulaic linking.
difficulties.response: Compare templated and disciplinary introductions and discuss their effect on readers. Do not ban formulaic language, which has legitimate uses; ask whether each phrase does its job.

difficulties.pattern: Writing opinion without sources ('In my opinion…') in assignments that require evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unsupported claims; feedback asking for evidence.
difficulties.response: Show the function of sources in university writing and practise supporting claims with them.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting university criteria to resemble generic test criteria.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners look for criteria such as 'lexical resource' in university rubrics.
difficulties.response: Compare a test criterion list with a disciplinary rubric, and link to genre families.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What did you do in your test essay that you should not do in a university essay, and why?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific habits (opinion without sources, templates, general topics) and explains the difference in task demands.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names one difference in general terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no difference or says only that university writing is longer.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses are the main sites for this topic, and it is core on both UG- and PG-route pre-sessionals; PG-route learners compare test tasks with master's assignments in their field. In-sessional UG and PGT learners who entered directly with a test score may need it in their first weeks, especially PGT learners with only a year to adjust.
reviewNotes: Moore and Morton's study concerns IELTS; other tests include integrated, source-based tasks, so the contrast is less sharp for them.
The IELTS Task 2 link was removed because the topic contrasts test tasks with university tasks (R6-11).

guidance.summary: Weigle (2002) discusses alternatives to timed impromptu writing, including portfolio and process-based assessment, which allow writing to be judged under conditions closer to academic practice; many pre-sessional programmes assess progression in this way through extended writing, projects and presentations. Bachman and Palmer (2010) highlight the consequences of assessment decisions for test takers, which are particularly significant in progression. Make components, weightings, criteria, thresholds and integrity rules explicit early, and build the course around formative stages.

activities.title: Progression map
learnerActions: Using your programme handbook, list each assessed component, its weighting and its criteria
Identify how results combine into the progression decision, including any minimum per skill
Mark the formative stages before each summative submission
Compare maps with a partner and check any uncertainty with your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Progression depends on several components and thresholds, and formative stages are the opportunities to improve.
activities.rationale: Making the assessment design visible lets learners plan effort and use formative feedback, which is how portfolio and process-based assessment is intended to work (Weigle, 2002).

activities.title: Draft-to-final tracker
learnerActions: Record the feedback you receive at each formative stage
Note the action you took on each comment
Before final submission, check that every priority comment has been addressed
activities.intendedInsight: Final performance in coursework-based progression depends heavily on how formative feedback is used.
activities.rationale: Process-based assessment rewards revision; tracking actions links progression assessment to feedback literacy.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the pre-sessional as test preparation and waiting for a final exam.
difficulties.revealedBy: Low engagement with drafts; questions about when 'the test' is.
difficulties.response: Explain the coursework-based design early and show how formative stages count towards the outcome.

difficulties.pattern: Over-investing in one component and neglecting others with minimum thresholds.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong essay, weak presentation or speaking result.
difficulties.response: Review the progression map at mid-course and rebalance effort.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about what help is permitted with drafts (peers, proofreaders, translation and AI tools).
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about using translation or AI tools, proofreaders or friends' help with drafts.
difficulties.response: Make the programme's integrity rules explicit with examples of permitted and non-permitted help, and ask learners to keep notes and drafts as a record of their process. A change of style between drafts is not evidence of misconduct on its own.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'How will your progression decision be made, and what is your weakest component?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes components, weightings and thresholds accurately and has a plan for the weakest component.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows the components but not the thresholds, or names a weak component with no plan.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know how progression is decided.

guidance.contextNotes: This is central on pre-sessional programmes. On UG-route courses, the extended project (see ges.extended-source-based-project) is often shorter and more scaffolded, and a timed integrated task is common; on PG-route courses, learners often choose a focus in their own field and present it orally. It is also relevant to foundation and pathway programmes with similar progression arrangements, and to bridging and direct-entry programmes outside the UK. Arrangements vary considerably between institutions.
reviewNotes: Progression arrangements vary widely; institutions that accept their own pre-sessional outcomes in place of a test for immigration purposes do so under specific regulatory conditions that change.

guidance.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) treat a score as evidence for a particular interpretation and use, which explains why the same report can satisfy one receiving body and not another: each institution or authority decides which tests, delivery modes, component profiles and test dates it accepts. Arkoudis et al. (2012) argue that entry standards mark the start of language development rather than its end, so test choice should also consider what the preparation will build. Rules on retakes, combined sittings, validity periods and at-home or remotely proctored versions differ between tests and receiving bodies and change often, and a visa route may set conditions different from a university's admission rules (for example, the UK Student route; UK Visas and Immigration, 2025). Teach learners to read a report against each condition and to verify every rule at source, not to memorise current rules.

activities.title: Report against requirement
learnerActions: Read a sample score report and note the overall score, each component score and the test date
Read a programme's English requirement page and list each condition (overall score, component minimums, accepted tests and delivery modes, validity, retake or combination rules)
Decide whether the report meets each condition on the programme's start date
Note which conditions you had to confirm in another official source, and which source
activities.intendedInsight: A score meets a requirement only if every condition is met, not just the overall score.
activities.rationale: A requirement is a decision rule applied to score evidence (Bachman & Palmer, 2010); checking each condition separately mirrors how receiving bodies apply it.

activities.title: Choosing a test from official sources
learnerActions: List the institutions, and any visa route, that will receive your score

For two tests you could take, collect from official pages only: acceptance by each receiving body, delivery modes, validity, retake and combination rules, cost and dates, noting the date you accessed each page
Compare the tests with your own skill profile and choose one, justifying the choice in three sentences
Check with a partner whether any part of your choice rests on an unofficial source
activities.intendedInsight: Test choice depends on what your receiving bodies accept now, which their official pages state and agents or forums may not.
activities.rationale: Score-use rules differ between receiving bodies and change; checking current official sources is more durable than learning specific rules, as visa guidance itself shows by being revised over time.

difficulties.pattern: 'My overall score is above the requirement, so I've met it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans or applications that overlook a component below the minimum.
difficulties.response: Work through profiles that pass overall but miss a component minimum, and have learners check each condition separately.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that a single-skill retake, a result combined from two sittings or an at-home version is accepted everywhere because the test owner offers it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners booking a format or retake without checking the receiving body's rules.
difficulties.response: Distinguish what a test owner offers from what each receiving body accepts, and require evidence from the receiving body's own page before booking.

difficulties.pattern: Requirement pages, agents and test owners give inconsistent or outdated information.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners citing conflicting rules, or rules that have since changed.
difficulties.response: Institutions should keep requirement pages dated, consistent and clear about which body's rule governs. Learners should record the date and source of each rule and, where sources conflict, ask the admissions office in writing before booking or submitting.

difficulties.pattern: Treating remote-proctoring and test-day rules (identity checks, room scans, no notes or second screens) as formalities.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about keeping notes nearby or using another device during an at-home test.
difficulties.response: Walk through the test owner's official candidate rules and the possible consequences, such as scores being withheld or cancelled. Learners who need adjustments (extra time, breaks, assistive technology) should request them through the test owner's process well in advance.

diagnostic.task: Give a programme requirement and a score report whose overall score meets it but which misses one component minimum and will be outside the stated validity period on the start date. Ask: 'Can this applicant use this score?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies both problems, names the official sources to check (the receiving body and the test owner) and suggests options, such as a retake if the receiving body accepts one.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Spots one problem, or spots both but would rely on an agent's advice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges by the overall score alone.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners use this when applying, when meeting conditional offers and when deciding between retesting and a longer pre-sessional; PG applicants more often hold older scores and need validity checks. Teach the process of reading and checking, and refer specific admissions or visa questions to the receiving body or qualified advisers rather than giving rules from memory. In EMI and TNE settings, local institutional tests or national examinations may stand in for international tests, so the receiving body's own list is the reference.
reviewNotes: Score-use rules (retakes, combined sittings, validity periods, accepted delivery modes) differ by test and receiving body and change often; the topic deliberately states no specific rule and should be reviewed at each release.
